summary: This document specifies version 3 of the RFC Editor Model. Policy is the joint responsibility of the RFC Series Working Group and the RFC Series Approval Board, while production and publishing are handled separately. It obsoletes RFC 9280 and updates several earlier RFCs.

plainLanguage.summary: This describes who decides the rules for RFCs and who does the work, like a school describing who writes the rules and who runs the office.

questions: what is the rfc editor model
what is the rfc series working group
subtitle: Who writes the rules for the RFC Series, who approves them, and who actually publishes the RFCs.

tldr.problem: The RFC Series needs clear authority, transparency and community input for deciding how RFCs are written and published, and the first version of this model (RFC 9280) needed fixes after real use.
tldr.mechanism: Policy definition is split between the open RFC Series Working Group (RSWG), which proposes, and the RFC Series Approval Board (RSAB), which approves. The RFC Production Center (RPC) implements policy under contract oversight by the IETF LLC, advised by the RFC Series Consulting Editor (RSCE).
tldr.outcome: Approved policies are published as Informational RFCs in a new Editorial Stream. This document obsoletes RFC 9280 and updates eleven other RFCs.

facts.label: Votes to approve despite a CONCERN

today: RFC 9920 is an Informational RFC published in February 2026. It obsoletes RFC 9280 and updates RFC 7841, RFC 9720 and other RFCs. No later RFC obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Two Tasks of the Model
sections.content:
Version 3 of the RFC Editor Model splits the work into two high-level tasks. Policy definition covers rules that govern the RFC Series as a whole, and is the joint responsibility of the RSWG and the RSAB. Policy implementation means publishing RFCs from all streams, which is primarily the job of the RPC, contractually overseen by the IETF Administration LLC (IETF LLC).

The RSCE provides expert advice to the RPC and RSAB. If the RPC meets problems applying a policy, it brings them to the RSAB, which interprets the policy and gives interim guidance. The RFC says the aim is public processes, clear lines of responsibility and effective operations.

The document is organized unusually: it keeps the section numbering of RFC 9280, so its Introduction is long and lists the changes from that RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two jobs: deciding the rules, and doing the printing. Different groups do each, and a helpful expert advises both.

sections.title: How Policy Is Defined
sections.content:
The RSWG is an open working group where anyone may take part, and its work follows rough consensus like IETF working groups. It has two chairs, one appointed by the IESG and one by the IAB. The RSAB approves proposals but has no independent power to write policy.

The RSAB has five voting members: stream representatives for the IETF, IAB, IRTF and Independent Streams, plus the RSCE. The IETF Executive Director and an RPC representative are non-voting members.

A proposal is an Internet-Draft that the RSWG adopts, develops and puts through a Last Call. The RSAB then issues a community call for comments, which lasts not less than two weeks. Each RSAB member then takes a position of YES, CONCERN or RECUSE. A proposal with no CONCERN is approved. Otherwise, after discussion, a vote is taken and at least three voting members must vote YES. Approved proposals are published as RFCs.

Appeals of RSWG chair decisions go to the RSAB, and appeals of RSAB decisions go to the IAB, in both cases within thirty days and only on specified grounds such as failure to follow process.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone can pitch a rule to the open club. When the club mostly agrees, the board asks everybody what they think and then votes. If enough board members say yes, the rule becomes official.

sections.title: Policy Implementation and the RPC
sections.content:
The RPC publishes RFCs and is advised by the RSCE and RSAB. The IETF LLC oversees it under contract and handles budget and vendor selection. This document does not fix the exact legal relationship, so the RPC could be a separate company, employees or contractors.

The RPC's duties include editing documents to the RFC Style Guide, assigning RFC numbers, coordinating with IANA, publishing and archiving RFCs, and running the errata system and the RFC Editor website. A key change from RFC 9280 is that the RPC is responsible for the tools and processes that implement Editorial Stream policy, and for detailed technical specifications such as text or graphical formats and XML grammar. It must document these decisions publicly, preferably with rationale.

If an author and the RPC disagree, the parties consult the relevant stream body or the RSAB. Disputes about tooling decisions now use the same appeal path to the RSAB.
sections.plainLanguage: The print shop does the actual editing and publishing and keeps its tools in order. If an author and the print shop disagree about a rule, the board settles it.

sections.title: The RSCE and the Editorial Stream
sections.content:
The RFC Series Consulting Editor is a senior technical publishing professional. The RSCE votes on the RSAB, spots problems and improvements in publication, and advises the RSWG, RPC and IETF LLC. The IETF LLC manages the RSCE's engagement, and a selection committee recommends who should hold the role.

The new Editorial Stream is used only for policies, procedures, guidelines and rules about the RFC Series as a whole. Everything it publishes has the status Informational, and it cannot publish Standards Track or Best Current Practice RFCs. Even so, these documents define policy for the Series. The RFC sets the Status of This Memo boilerplate for the stream and requires the usual patent and trademark disclosure rules of the Internet-Draft process.
sections.plainLanguage: The expert editor gives advice and has a vote. The special "Editorial Stream" is a shelf just for rule books about how the whole library works.

sections.title: Historical Properties and Changes from Version 2
sections.content:
Section 7 lists properties long valued in the Series: availability, accessibility, English-language publication with translation permitted, diversity of document types, quality, stability, longevity and consistency. Proposals that could harm them need heightened scrutiny.

Two properties changed in this document. On stability, published RFCs may now be reissued, but their semantic content shall be preserved as far as possible (see RFC 9720). A new consistency property says RFCs may be reissued to keep presentation consistent.

Compared with version 2, the RFC Editor function is spread across the RSWG, RSAB, RPC, RSCE and IETF LLC. The RFC Series Oversight Committee is dispensed with, the RSAG is disbanded, and references to the RFC Series Editor should be read as the RFC Editor function, not the RSCE. Earlier versions are RFC 5620 (version 1) and RFC 6635 (version 2).
sections.plainLanguage: The library keeps its old promises, such as free access and readable books. It now allows reprinting a book as long as the meaning stays the same.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 8729 apply. Publication processes must prevent unapproved changes, and because several entities, especially the RPC, help maintain the publication index, enough security is needed to stop outsiders changing published documents. The archive, source documents and related originals such as errata lists need protection against data storage failure.

The RPC coordinates with IANA so RFCs accurately record registries and assigned values. This document creates no registry and needs no IANA action.
sections.plainLanguage: The library must stop anyone from secretly changing its books and must keep backup copies in case something breaks.
